passage: The dairy society office in the kasba smelled of milk cans and damp registers. Jyoti had been there four months, and Farooq had been kind since the first week. He had found her a room and shown her the shortcut to the bus stand. So when she saw him shaving a little off the weights in the morning register, she stared at the page for a long time. Her chest felt tight. That evening she waited by the tea stall. "Farooq bhai, the entries don't match the scale. You need to fix them." He laughed, then looked away. "Everyone does it, it's small." "It's not small if it's the farmers' milk," she said, her voice shaking. "You have until Friday. After that I will have to tell the secretary." He said nothing, and she walked home wondering if she'd lost a friend.

qa.q: How long had Jyoti been at the dairy society office?
qa.a: Jyoti had been there four months.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when she saw Farooq shaving the weights?
qa.a: Torn and tense: her chest felt tight, she stared at the page a long time, and she wondered if she had lost a friend.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do that balanced loyalty and honesty?
qa.a: She spoke to Farooq privately, asked him to fix the entries by Friday and said she would tell the secretary afterwards.

qa.q: How might Farooq have felt hearing Jyoti's words at the tea stall?
qa.a: Probably embarrassed and defensive, since he laughed, looked away and said everyone does it.

grounding: The wrongdoer is a friend who helped her settle in; she feels torn, gives him a chance to correct it, and sets a limit on silence.

passage: Sneha, since you asked about speaking up late, listen. I'm Bhavna, and at twenty-one, in my first lab job, I noticed that Kunal bhaiya, the senior technician, was ticking off the eye-wash checks on the safety log when the station was actually broken. I said nothing. I told myself it was small, he was senior, someone else would notice. By March the whole shift was copying the tick marks and the log said things that weren't true. My stomach was in knots every morning. One day I walked into the lab head's room and said, "I saw this in January and I should have said so then. Here are the dates." Her face changed, but she thanked me. The station was fixed within days. Being late was awkward. Staying silent because I'd already stayed silent would have been worse.

qa.q: What did Kunal bhaiya tick off on the safety log while the station was broken?
qa.a: He ticked off the eye-wash checks.

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel as the false log grew?
qa.a: Uneasy and guilty: her stomach was in knots every morning and she kept telling herself it was small.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do that was right, even though it was late?
qa.a: She went to the lab head, admitted she had seen it in January and gave the dates so the facts could lead.

qa.q: How might the lab head have felt hearing Bhavna's account?
qa.a: Probably concerned and surprised, since her face changed, but grateful, since she thanked Bhavna and the station was fixed in days.

grounding: An elder recalls noticing something wrong earlier and saying nothing; guilt grew as the problem did, until the protagonist spoke up and acknowledged the delay.

passage: Kwame had reported the blocked fire exit in his Leeds hall of residence back in October. It was now February, and the door was still chained. He had emailed the housing office twice and got the same auto-reply both times. "They don't care," he told Rania in the kitchen, jabbing at a slice of toast. "It's the same everywhere. What's the point?" Rania, the peer adviser from the students' union, leaned on the counter. "The housing office isn't the only route. There's the union's advice service, and a formal complaints process with a deadline." "You believe that works?" "Sometimes. It took me two tries once." That night Kwame wrote out the dates, attached the photos he'd taken, and sent it to the union adviser. Three weeks later the chain was gone, and Kwame stood in the doorway a moment, a little surprised.

qa.q: Where was the blocked fire exit that Kwame reported?
qa.a: It was in his Leeds hall of residence.

qa.q: How did Kwame feel about systems after the housing office's replies?
qa.a: Cynical and discouraged, as he said they don't care and asked what the point was.

qa.q: What did Kwame do that worked when the first channel failed?
qa.a: He took a different route, sending his dated report and photos to the union's advice service.

qa.q: What is it like for Rania when Kwame says the process is pointless?
qa.a: Rania probably feels a mix of understanding and hope, since Rania admits it once took two tries yet still believes it can work.

grounding: The protagonist reported and nothing happened, feels cynical about systems, then tries another channel with help from people who know the process.

passage: Mentor's note, Friday. Aditi asked to speak to me after the team meeting. Two weeks ago she raised a concern about the delivery reports, and things have been tense since. In the pantry yesterday, I noticed, several colleagues slipped her small thank-yous. Ishita, from another desk, said quietly, "I'm glad you said it. I couldn't." Aditi told me her hands were shaking after, but she stood straighter. "It helped more than I expected," she said. She also said she doesn't expect any of them to speak up in the room. "They have their own reasons and their own risks," she said. "I don't want Ishita to feel bad for keeping quiet." I told her it was a mature way to hold it. I've noted the concern for follow-up, and I'll check in next Friday.

qa.q: Who told Aditi in the pantry, "I'm glad you said it. I couldn't"?
qa.a: Ishita, from another desk, said it.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel after the colleagues thanked her?
qa.a: Encouraged and braver: her hands were shaking, but she stood straighter and said it helped more than she expected.

qa.q: What did Aditi do that protected both herself and her colleagues?
qa.a: She valued the support without expecting public backing and made sure not to make Ishita feel guilty for staying quiet.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel about thanking Aditi?
qa.a: Possibly relieved to show support in a quiet way, and perhaps uneasy about not speaking up, which is why the thanks came with "I couldn't."

grounding: Colleagues quietly thank the protagonist for speaking up, which gives courage, while she does not pressure them to stand publicly.

passage: The supermarket closed in fifteen minutes and the last bus left in twenty, and Arohi was standing in front of the bins in the entrance, holding a bottle and a jar. Which one was for glass? She had already been scolded once, in her second week, by a neighbour for putting paper in the wrong bin, and the memory made her ears burn. All the labels were in German. Kamal, a neighbour from the flat below, appeared beside her with his trolley. "It's confusing, isn't it? Brown for glass here. Ask, everyone does." Arohi laughed, shakily. He told her about a language cafe on Thursday evenings where newcomers practise with locals. "Come. Bring your questions." She caught the bus with eight minutes to spare, already writing Thursday in her phone.

qa.q: Which colour bin did Kamal say is for glass?
qa.a: Kamal said brown is for glass.

qa.q: What was Arohi afraid of at the bins?
qa.a: Making another mistake with the rules, since her ears burned at the memory of being scolded for the wrong bin.

qa.q: What small steps helped Arohi in this situation?
qa.a: She asked for help, accepted Kamal's advice and planned to go to the Thursday language cafe to learn with others.

qa.q: How might Kamal see Arohi's confusion at the bins?
qa.a: As ordinary for a newcomer, since Kamal said it is confusing and that everyone asks.

grounding: In a new country the protagonist fears mistakes with language and rules; asking, watching and finding a small community makes her feel steadier.

passage: In the small town, everyone smiled at Jyoti. The shopkeeper said good morning, the neighbours nodded, and the women at the water tap made room for her. But nobody ever said, "Come for tea." Jyoti, posted here as a schoolteacher from another state, heard her own accent bend around the local words and felt like a guest who had overstayed. That evening she decided perhaps the whole town simply disliked outsiders. Then Rehana, the maths teacher, mentioned that the library reading circle needed someone for the Saturday session. Jyoti went. She kept going, too: the reading circle, the temple fair, small talk at the vegetable stall. Five weeks in, the tap-women asked about her mother. It was small. But it was a start.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do in the town as a schoolteacher?
qa.a: Jyoti was posted there as a schoolteacher from another state.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel among the smiling townspeople?
qa.a: She felt lonely and out of place, like a guest who had overstayed, since everyone was polite but nobody invited her in.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do that helped her begin to belong?
qa.a: She kept showing up at the reading circle, the temple fair and the vegetable stall, making small talk.

qa.q: How might Rehana see Jyoti's place in town?
qa.a: Rehana may see a newcomer whom the town hasn't yet had chance to know, which is why Rehana mentioned the reading circle.

grounding: People are polite but never invite the protagonist in and her accent makes her feel an outsider; she keeps showing up and belonging builds slowly.

passage: The call from home came just as Tariq's friend Liam was pulling on his football boots. "You never talk to us now," his mother said, a little sharply. Tariq wasn't sure what he felt. He'd stopped calling every evening, he'd begun laughing at Liam's jokes in a way that felt new, and last month he had eaten a full pub dinner without thinking twice. He was sitting on the bench in a Dublin park with the phone against his ear, and guilt pressed on him. Was he leaving something behind? Then he said, "Amma, I miss your rice more than anything. And I like it here too. I can be both." There was a pause. "Bring your friend to dinner when you come home," she said. Liam waved from the pitch.

qa.q: Where was Tariq sitting when his mother called?
qa.a: Tariq was sitting on a bench in a Dublin park.

qa.q: What was Tariq feeling as he held the phone against his ear?
qa.a: Guilt: he wondered if he was leaving something behind as he adapted to new ways.

qa.q: What did Tariq do that worked better than hiding one half?
qa.a: He told his mother honestly that he misses her rice and likes it in Dublin too, and that he can be both.

qa.q: How might Tariq's mother have felt hearing "I can be both"?
qa.a: Probably relieved and reassured, since she went from sharp to inviting Liam to dinner.

grounding: The protagonist adapts to new ways and feels guilt towards his parents' culture, then explains that he can hold both.

passage: Alejandro turned the shower on high so the flatmates wouldn't hear him cry. He missed his grandmother's kitchen, the noise of Spanish across a table, the smell of beans cooking at noon. In Cape Town the sun set at the wrong time and everything tasted of nothing. Afterwards he felt foolish, as though he ought to be tougher. Zanele found him staring at the stove the next evening. "Homesick? I was in Durban for a year before I stopped feeling it." She helped him find dried chillies at the market and they cooked a big pot of beans. He'd also put Sunday calls with his grandmother in his phone, and on Thursday he went to a potluck of Latin American students. It was still sad in places. But the ache was easier to carry with others.

qa.q: Why did Alejandro turn the shower on high?
qa.a: So the flatmates wouldn't hear him cry.

qa.q: How did Alejandro feel about crying in the shower afterwards?
qa.a: Foolish, as though he ought to be tougher.

qa.q: What did Alejandro do to ease the homesickness?
qa.a: He scheduled Sunday calls with his grandmother, cooked a familiar pot of beans with Zanele and joined a potluck of Latin American students.

qa.q: How might Zanele see Alejandro's homesickness?
qa.a: As normal and something that eases with time, since she recalls feeling it herself for a year.

grounding: The protagonist misses home food, language and family and cries in secret; calls, familiar cooking and fellow migrants make it easier to carry.

passage: On Friday evening the community centre's common room buzzed with Telugu, steam from the biryani and a cricket match on the wall screen. Akash stood in the doorway with his rucksack still on. "Come in, come in!" Jahnavi, the society's secretary, pulled out a chair. "First month is always the hardest." Within ten minutes somebody had asked which town he was from, somebody else had passed him a plate, and his shoulders finally dropped for the first time since the flight. He felt safe. On the walk home he thought, I could spend every evening here and never learn how to buy a bus pass. So on Monday he said yes to his lab partner's invitation to the chemistry club, and the next month he brought her to the society's dinner.

qa.q: What was showing on the common room's wall screen?
qa.a: A cricket match was showing.

qa.q: How did Akash feel after ten minutes in the common room?
qa.a: Safe and relaxed, as his shoulders dropped for the first time since the flight.

qa.q: What did Akash do that added to the comfort of his community?
qa.a: He also said yes to the chemistry club and later brought his lab partner to the society dinner.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see Akash's arrival at the community centre?
qa.a: As a newcomer in his hardest first month who needs a warm welcome, since Jahnavi pulled out a chair for him.

grounding: Others from the protagonist's home community welcome him warmly and he feels safe, while he also builds friendships beyond it.

passage: In the library booth on the third floor, Payal held her phone up so her mother could see the shelves. "Look at my Payal, in a foreign library!" her mother told a neighbour on speaker. "She's sending a photo of her big flat next week, isn't that right, beta?" Payal smiled. "Yes, Mummy." In reality she shared a room the width of a corridor and skipped dinner on Thursdays. When the call ended she sat with her head in her hands. Vandana, from the next booth, slid a coffee across. "That sounded heavy." Payal told her everything. The next Sunday she said gently to her mother, "It's a hard time, Mummy. I'm working part-time and the room is tiny. I'm doing well, but not the way you tell people." Her mother was quiet, then said, "Tell me more."

qa.q: Who slid a coffee across to Payal after the call?
qa.a: Vandana did.

qa.q: How did Payal feel while her mother boasted to the neighbour?
qa.a: A gap between the picture and reality, and heavy, since she smiled and said yes then sat with her head in her hands.

qa.q: What did Payal do that set more realistic expectations?
qa.a: She told her mother gently about the part-time work and tiny room, without pretending everything was perfect.

qa.q: How might Payal's mother have felt on hearing the honest version?
qa.a: Possibly surprised and worried, but the quiet and the words "Tell me more" suggest she wanted to understand.

grounding: The protagonist's family boasts about life abroad and expects success stories; she feels the gap and shares honest difficulties gently.
